title: The Gospel of Mark
lead: The shortest and, on most scholars' view, the earliest Gospel, credited from the early 100s to Mark, often identified with John Mark of Acts and with Peter's interpreter. It tells the story of God's Son as a story of hiddenness, misunderstanding and the cross.

sections.h: John Mark in the New Testament
sections.b: "John, also called Mark" was the son of a Mary whose house in Jerusalem was a meeting place of the early church; Peter went there when he escaped from prison (Acts 12:12). He traveled with Barnabas, his cousin (Colossians 4:10), and Paul to Cyprus, but left them at Perga (Acts 13:5, 13). Paul refused to take him on the next journey, and Barnabas and Paul parted over it (Acts 15:37–39). Later Paul calls him a fellow worker (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24) and "useful to me for ministry" (2 Timothy 4:11). 1 Peter 5:13 sends greetings from "my son Mark" in "Babylon," a common Christian name for Rome. Whether all these refer to one man, and whether he wrote the Gospel, is debated; the name Marcus was very common.
sections.refs: Acts 12:12; Acts 12:25; Acts 13:5; Acts 13:13; Acts 15:37–39; Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11; 1 Peter 5:13

sections.b: The earliest statement about the Gospel comes from Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, early in the 100s, quoted by Eusebius (Church History 3.39.15): Mark, who had become Peter's interpreter, wrote down accurately but "not in order" what he remembered of the Lord's words and deeds, as Peter had taught them to meet the needs of his hearers. Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria repeat the link with Peter and place the writing in Rome. Critics ask whether Papias was defending a Gospel whose order differed from others; defenders such as Martin Hengel and Richard Bauckham argue that the tradition is early and fits the Gospel's focus on Peter (Mark 1:16; Mark 16:7).

Mark's Jesus repeatedly commands silence about who he is: to demons (Mark 1:25, 34; 3:12), to those he heals (Mark 1:44; 5:43; 7:36; 8:26) and to his disciples (Mark 8:30; 9:9). William Wrede (1901) named this the "messianic secret" and argued it was the early church's way of explaining why Jesus was not recognized as Messiah in his lifetime. Others see historical caution (Jesus avoided titles that would sound like a call to revolt) or a theological point: Jesus' identity can be understood only in the light of the cross and resurrection (Mark 9:9). The secret is often broken (Mark 1:45; 7:36), which suggests that Mark's interest is less in hiding the truth than in showing what kind of Messiah Jesus is.
sections.refs: Mark 1:25; Mark 1:34; Mark 1:44–45; Mark 3:12; Mark 5:43; Mark 7:36; Mark 8:26; Mark 8:30; Mark 9:9

sections.b: Mark often starts one story, inserts another, and then finishes the first, so that each sheds light on the other. Examples: Jesus' family and the scribes (Mark 3:20–35), Jairus' daughter and the bleeding woman (Mark 5:21–43), the mission of the Twelve and the death of John (Mark 6:7–30), the fig tree and the Temple (Mark 11:12–25), the plot and the anointing (Mark 14:1–11), Peter's denial and Jesus' trial (Mark 14:54–72). James Edwards and others have shown how the technique carries Mark's meaning.

Mark was long overshadowed by Matthew; Augustine thought Mark had abridged it. In the 1800s Mark came to be seen by most scholars as the earliest Gospel and a source for Matthew and Luke (see the topic on the Synoptic problem). In Christian art Mark is the lion of the four living creatures (Ezekiel 1:10; Revelation 4:7). The church of Alexandria, and the Coptic Orthodox Church after it, honors Mark as founder and first bishop (Eusebius, Church History 2.16); Venetian merchants took his relics from Alexandria to Venice in 828, and the winged lion of Saint Mark became Venice's emblem. His feast is April 25.
